summary:
OpenAtlas: see the infrared sky change

OpenAtlas is a free, open-source web app that turns NASA's SPHEREx survey into a tool anyone can use to search for moving and changing objects in the sky. You enter a star's name or any coordinates, and OpenAtlas gathers every SPHEREx exposure of that spot from NASA's IRSA archive. It lines the frames up on a common north-up grid, and lets you blink them like a flip-book, stack them, or subtract them to reveal what changed.

It then goes further. It measures each source's brightness over time (light curves) and across 102 infrared colours (spectra). It flags candidate movers and variables and cross-checks them against Gaia and WISE.

This answers the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge directly. Faint, cold, fast-moving objects like brown dwarfs, or an undiscovered planet, show up best in infrared and give themselves away by moving between exposures.

A Learning Hub, guided tours and plain-language hints make this possible without an astronomy degree. Every view is a shareable link, and the code is AGPL-licensed. OpenAtlas opens real NASA data to students and citizen scientists who could make the next discovery.
details:
What it. How it works

OpenAtlas is a web app that lets you see how the infrared sky changes over time using real data from NASAs SPHEREx mission. You type a stars name or any coordinates. OpenAtlas asks NASAs IRSA archive for every SPHEREx exposure covering that spot more than 250 of them and downloads only a small cut‑out around the target from each one. It then lines all the frames up on a north‑up grid using their exact sky coordinates. You can blink the frames like a flip‑book so anything that moves or changes stands out stack them to reveal sources or subtract early frames from late frames so only what changed remains. OpenAtlas also measures brightness in every frame giving curves over a year of data and spectra across SPHERExs 102 infrared colours (0.75 to 5 µm). OpenAtlas automatically flags candidate movers and variable stars and cross‑checks them against the Gaia DR3 and AllWISE catalogues so users know at once whether something is already known.

Benefits and intended impact

SPHEREx maps the sky but working with its raw data normally needs special software and expertise. OpenAtlas removes that barrier: it runs in any browser needs no installation and explains itself. A Learning Hub teaches the four core ideas (blink, stack, difference, stretch) with examples. Every page has a guided tour and plain‑language hints sit next to every control. Every view is a link so a student can send a teacher exactly what they found. OpenAtlas lets students, teachers and citizen scientists take part in discovery work. Cold, faint fast‑moving objects such as brown dwarfs or a hypothetical distant planet are brightest in the infrared and show up by moving between exposures. That is what the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge asks for.

Tools and technologies

The backend is written in Python with FastAPI. It uses Astropy for coordinates and image alignment NumPy and SciPy for image processing and Pillow for rendering. Data comes from NASA/IPAC IRSAs SIA2 and cut‑out services, the Gaia DR3 and AllWISE catalogues via VizieR and CDS Sesame for name resolution. The frontend is built with React and Vite with Aladin Lite for the all‑sky map of SPHERExs 102‑channel data cube. The app is hosted in the cloud on Render; during development we ran it on a Windows server with Cloudflare. The demo video was made with Remotion. OpenAtlas is source under the GNU AGPL‑3.0.

What makes it creative

of building a data download tool we treated the sky as something to watch. Blinking is the technique astronomers used to discover Pluto. We rebuilt it for a 102‑colour infrared survey and made it usable by anyone. We also handled the cases honestly. Bright stars saturate SPHERExs detectors so OpenAtlas estimates their brightness, from the outer glow and labels it clearly. If NASAs archive is temporarily down the app says so and marks any demo data instead of failing silently.

Factors we considered

honesty: candidates are presented as candidates never as discoveries with confidence values and catalogue cross‑checks. Accessibility: language, keyboard shortcuts, readable contrast and a layout that works on phones. Performance: data is downloaded once. Cached and only the needed cut‑outs are fetched. Openness: the code is free, public and documented so others can verify, reuse and extend OpenAtlas.
